title: TypeScript with React and JSX knowledge check

questions.prompt: What should a typed frontend still validate?
options: User input and server responses at runtime, while keeping loading, success and failure states explicit.
Nothing: JSX and TypeScript guarantee every browser value is valid.
The frontend can decide server authorization by itself.
Only CSS class names need types.
questions.answer_key: User input and server responses at runtime, while keeping loading, success and failure states explicit.
questions.explanation: Typed UI models improve development feedback but do not replace runtime validation or server-side checks.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “TypeScript with React and JSX”?
options: The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
The concept should be demonstrated with .tsx files and checked against its intended contract.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with .tsx files and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “.tsx files”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “TypeScript with React and JSX”?
options: Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
Check component props, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
Assume typing events, state, and reusable components is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
questions.answer_key: Check component props, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “Component props”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
